summary.title: We gave AI agents a mobile dev environment
summary.idea: Mobile agents were limited by laptop resources and Linux lacking iOS tooling, so Shopify gave each agent session a remote, pre-warmed Mac with an emulator and a skill that teaches it to prove its work.
howItWorks: Keep a pool of warm Macs with main checked out, tools installed and apps built, cutting setup from 30+ minutes to minutes.
Each agent claims a Mac over SSH, syncs its branch, and attaches a prebuilt Android VM for testing.
A CLI wraps the fiddly SSH flags, and tmux panes let the agent watch long-running tasks instead of sleeping.
A skill tells the agent to reproduce a bug, record it, fix it, then record the same steps again for before and after.
A cheap classifier tags every mobile conversation by outcome, and failures feed an LLM that improves the skill.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent says it can't verify something, write a skill plus a small CLI wrapper that gives it a remote environment and requires before-and-after screenshots or recordings with every fix.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building remote environments for agents that must build and test real apps, or want a concrete loop for improving agent skills from failed sessions.
summary.quote: So we created a skill to teach agents how to test their changes and prove their work.

verdict.reason: Shopify walks through its working mobile agent harness, and the page supports every card claim: a warm Mac pool, a CLI wrapping SSH, tmux panes the agent watches instead of sleeping, before-and-after recordings as proof, and failed sessions classified to improve the skill; it loses points because there is no code and the infrastructure is heavy for most teams to copy.

summary.title: Context Engineering Starts with Retrieval
summary.idea: Agents burn their limited context on clumsy searches, oversized results and stale or irrelevant text; the fix is cheap search first, results saved to files, and subagents doing the reading.
howItWorks: Search before reading: glob matches file names, grep finds matching lines, and read_file pages through 100 lines at a time.
Oversized tool results (over about 20,000 tokens) are saved to a file; the agent gets the path plus a short preview.
A custom retrieval tool writes each hit to a file and returns only the paths, not the full text.
A chunk-analyst subagent reads one retrieved file each, in parallel, and returns key facts with the source URL.
Filter by date or use a search API for freshness, and check that answers cite the expected sources.
summary.stealThis: Next time you build a RAG or search tool for an agent, make it save each result to a file and return only the paths, then hand each path to a subagent that summarises it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a research-style agent whose context fills up with search results, and want working code for the retrieve, offload, delegate pattern.

verdict.reason: Teaches a transferable 'retrieve, offload, delegate' pattern with working code: a retrieval tool writes hits to files and returns only paths, and per-file subagents return key facts with sources; it docks for being framed around LangChain's Deep Agents harness, though the pattern ports to any harness.

summary.title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary.idea: Shared team agents need more than a prompt: LangChain's internal agents for sales, engineering and marketing all rely on the same five building blocks, including per-person identity and scoped memory.
howItWorks: Put the agent in the team's chat tool, with its own app, so people can DM or tag it.
Split identity: act as the invoking user for personal tools, and use fixed credentials for shared services.
Limit risky tools by context, such as email only in DMs and posting rights for whitelisted users.
Keep two memory tiers, global and per-user, and let the agent choose where each fact goes.
Run code in a sandbox with a secret proxy, and trigger many runs by schedule or event.
summary.stealThis: Before you give a team agent access to real services, list each tool and mark it as acting as the user or as the agent, then hide the user-identity tools in shared channels.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're rolling out one agent to a whole team and need to decide identity, memory and scheduling, and can tolerate a LangChain-flavored tooling pitch.
summary.quote: It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others

verdict.reason: The page teaches transferable patterns for multiplayer agents, such as splitting tools into on-behalf-of-user versus fixed-credential identity, hiding user-identity tools outside DMs, whitelisting risky operations and two-tier memory, though it offers no code or before/after evidence and ends in a Managed Deep Agents pitch.

summary.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here's Why.
summary.idea: Models solve hard problems when a harness lets them run many cheap depth-first attempts, prunes them with a verifier, and feeds every failure back as a negative hint.
howItWorks: A drafter writes solver prompts from model priors plus a running list of failed approaches, which act as negative hints.
A solver runs one or many candidate attempts, using parallel subagents to pursue different paths to completion.
A verifier checks finished arguments automatically, so spending compute on uncertain ideas becomes rational.
Prompts add standing adversarial checks for known failure modes, plus a line telling the model not to quit when approaches fail.
Predict where this works: problems with few key insights and a small branching factor at each step.
summary.stealThis: Next time an agent task keeps failing, add a drafter step that rewrites the prompt each round with a list of what already failed and why, plus standing checks for those failure modes.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building multi-agent loops with verifiers and want a mental model for which problems are worth pointing them at.
summary.quote: Every one of these lines is a failed path, written up as an instruction.

verdict.reason: The essay is mostly analysis of why models succeed at math, but it does teach a transferable drafter/solver/verifier loop: fold each failed attempt back into the next prompt as a negative hint and promote known failure modes to standing adversarial checks, backed by the quoted CDC prompt. The setup is the author's reconstruction of what OpenAI likely did, not a demonstrated harness, so the technique is thin.

summary.title: Make coding agents prove their work
summary.idea: An agent's own summary describes what it meant to do, not what happened, so require checkable evidence in every report and enforce the fast checks with a Stop hook.
howItWorks: Run checks cheapest first: typecheck, lint, build with prerender, bundle budget, then screenshots at desktop and phone widths.
Every report must include changed files, pasted command output, test counts, budget numbers, screenshot paths, and a section on what was not checked.
A Claude Code Stop hook runs typecheck and lint; exit code 2 returns errors to the agent so it keeps working.
The hook checks the stop_hook_active flag and allows one forced retry, avoiding endless loops on unfixable errors.
A CI budget script gzips the initial JS and CSS, fails above 250 KB, and prints numbers on every build.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task, add a Stop hook that runs typecheck and lint and exits 2 on failure, and require the report to end with a 'what I did not check' section.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent changes on trust and want the full hook script, budget check and Playwright screenshot script to copy.
summary.quote: An agent's summary of its own work is the least reliable part of its output

verdict.reason: The page teaches concrete verification techniques with full code: a Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2 on typecheck or lint failure and uses a stop_hook_active guard against loops, a mandatory evidence report with a 'what I did not check' section, a gzip bundle budget in CI, and Playwright screenshots at two widths, all of which the card accurately reflects.

summary.title: An agent PR that only says 'fixed' makes the reviewer redo the diagnosis
summary.idea: Agent PRs that just say 'done, tests pass' force reviewers to re-derive the bug; a fixed PR template demanding reproduction and before/after evidence makes the claim checkable in minutes.
howItWorks: Use a PR template with blank fields: reproduction, before/after check, touched scope, uncovered assumptions, and revert and risk.
The reproduction field holds the exact failing command, the expected result and the actual result.
Name the check that failed and now passes, and say whether it was newly added or already existed.
Add 'repro command present' and 'failing check named' to the agent's done-checklist so empty fields block completion.
Before accepting 'done', ask the agent to paste the failing log line and the command that reproduced it.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-opened pull request, add a template with reproduction, before/after check, scope and assumptions fields, and have the agent refuse to mark done while any is blank.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck on reviewing agent pull requests and keep re-running failures to confirm a fix is real.
summary.quote: A green suite proves the current checks pass; it rarely proves the specific bug that broke is closed.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: an evidence-based agent PR template (repro command, before/after check, scope, assumptions, revert) wired into the done-checklist, plus a cheap 'paste the failing log line' check, but it's short and has no real example template, repo or before/after.

summary.title: Your AI Agent Says “Done.” What Did It Actually Verify?
summary.idea: Agents report 'done' with confident summaries that are not proof, so define observable acceptance criteria up front and require a completion report listing the exact checks run, results and what stayed unverified.
howItWorks: State the expected behavior as an observable outcome before the agent starts, including a regression test requirement.
Require a completion report: what changed, commands run, pass or fail results, and what could not be checked.
Confirm the new regression test fails against the original code and passes after the fix.
Scrutinize test edits such as skipped tests, removed assertions, swapped mocks, or changed expected values.
Treat blocked checks as unfinished verification and complete them elsewhere before relying on the result.
summary.stealThis: Paste the post's reusable completion-report prompt into your next agent coding task, asking for exact checks run, test changes made, and what remains unverified, then review the test diff separately before merging.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent-written code and want a checklist plus a reusable prompt for spotting weak or fake verification, with useful pitfalls in the comments.
summary.quote: A command mentioned in a summary is still a claim until you can confirm its execution.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: upfront observable acceptance criteria plus a reusable completion-report prompt (exact checks run, fail-first regression test, test-edit disclosure, unverified list), and the card accurately reflects the page, though the evidence is a small illustrative example rather than a real repo or before-and-after.

summary.title: The State of Context Engineering
summary.idea: Long-running agents get stuck on bad context, fixated ideas, and stale memory; the answer is a small set of harness moves like loadout, quarantine, pruning, offloading and periodic context resets.
howItWorks: Tool loadout: a fast small model checks each tool against the request and exposes only the relevant subset.
Quarantine: wrap a subagent as a tool so it starts with a blank history in the same environment.
Pruning and pre-compaction filtering: a small model flags old turns as still needed or not, then you summarize what remains.
Against context inertia, write a short note every ninety minutes or so and clear the conversation, keeping files and artifacts.
Treat repeated, all-caps instructions in a prompt as a sign you are fighting the model's training.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent loops on one idea or acts oddly past about 200,000 tokens, have it write a handoff note to a file, clear the context, and restart from that note.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building or tuning an agent harness and want the failure modes behind context rot, plus the short DSPy sketches showing each fix.
summary.quote: Our output is the product of the context and the weights.

verdict.reason: The talk teaches concrete harness moves the page actually describes: small-model tool loadout, subagent quarantine, per-turn pruning, filter-before-compaction, and periodic note-and-clear resets against context inertia, backed by cited papers and short DSPy sketches, though the code itself isn't shown in the text.

summary.title: Spec-Driven Development with AI Coding Agents: Specs, Tasks, Security
summary.idea: Agent output is hard to review when intent lives only in chat; writing requirements, design and task files first, with testable EARS criteria and security rules, makes review cheaper and checkable.
howItWorks: The agent drafts requirements, design and tasks files; a human approves each phase before the next begins.
Write each acceptance criterion in EARS form, so it maps to a test setup, action and assertion.
Tag criteria with versioned OWASP ASVS IDs and keep project-wide rules in AGENTS.md or a constitution.
List approved dependencies with pinned versions in the spec, and let CI fail on any unapproved direct dependency.
Define a task as done only when its linked test passes in CI, and update the spec in the same pull request.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-built feature, write each acceptance criterion as 'If [trigger], then the [system] shall [response]' with an ID, and require the agent's test names to carry those IDs.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing large agent diffs and want a full worked spec, task list and CI check to copy.
summary.quote: A ticked box in tasks.md is an assertion, not proof.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a tool-agnostic spec-first workflow with a full worked example: EARS acceptance criteria with IDs mapped to setup, action and assertion, requirement IDs in test names, an approved-dependency list, and a copyable CI job that fails on unapproved direct dependencies; the Safeguard marketing is incidental, and the card matches the page accurately.
